property_summary: Calls to lockInGuess must revert when called with any value not equal to 1 ether (i.e., only calls sending exactly 1 ether may succeed).
lockInGuess succeeds (does not revert) if and only if the sent value equals 1 ether
Any call to lockInGuess that sends a value different from 1 ether must revert (i.e., reverted == (amount != 1 ether)).
In the original contract, any call to lockInGuess that does not send exactly 1 ether must revert, so if a caller sends an amount different from 1 ether then the call always reverts (in M it may not).

Reference contract C requires callers to send exactly 1 ether when calling lockInGuess, so for any caller who has not already locked in a guess a call to lockInGuess with value != 1 ether will revert (preventing the guess from being recorded); the mutant removing the msg.value==1 ether check allows calls with other values to succeed and therefore will record guesses for some inputs (amounts) that the reference rejects.

For any caller and any provided bytes32 input, the reference contract stores exactly the provided hash (guesses[addr].guess == hash) when lockInGuess is called; the mutant instead stores keccak256(hash) for some inputs, so there exist inputs where the stored value differs.

For any caller and any bytes32 input, after calling lockInGuess(hash) successfully the reference contract stores exactly that provided hash for the caller (guesses[caller].guess == hash); the mutant instead stores keccak256(hash) causing a mismatch for inputs where keccak256(hash) != hash.

For every caller and every bytes32 value x, after a successful lockInGuess(x) the reference contract stores guesses[caller].guess == x (the mutant stores keccak256(x) instead, so for inputs where keccak256(x) != x the stored value differs).

For any caller and any bytes32 guess provided to lockInGuess, the correct contract stores a guess value equal to keccak256(abi.encodePacked(guesser, hash, block.number + 1)) derived from caller, provided hash and assigned block (so it's unique and depends on caller+input+block); the mutant that stores keccak256(hash) breaks this rule for some inputs because it omits caller+block in the stored commitment.

For every caller and any bytes32 input, after a successful lockInGuess(hash) the stored guess equals the keccak256(abi.encodePacked(hash, uint256(block.number + 1))) in the reference (tying the stored value to the provided hash and the scheduled block), but the mutant that stores keccak256(hash) (omitting the block) will violate this for some inputs and block numbers.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with 1 ether when they have no pending guess, the contract stores the supplied guess value in the public mapping (so the stored guess equals the argument); the mutant clears the guess to zero so this property is broken for inputs where the provided guess is non-zero.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether when they have no prior guess, the contract stores the provided bytes32 hash in the public mapping (guesses[caller].guess == providedHash); the mutant instead stores zero and thus violates this for inputs where the provided hash is non-zero.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether when they have no prior guess, the contract stores the provided bytes32 hash in the public mapping; the mutant instead stores zero so there exists an input (a caller and nonzero hash) where the stored guess differs (bug breaks this rule).

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether when they have no prior guess, the contract's public stored guess for that caller equals the provided bytes32 hash; the mutant instead stores zero so this equality can be violated for inputs where the provided hash is non-zero.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether when they have no prior guess, the contract's public stored guess for that caller is either equal to the provided bytes32 hash or (if the provided hash is zero) equal to zero; the mutant always stores zero so there exist inputs with a non-zero provided hash where stored guess != provided hash (violating equality).

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess sending exactly 1 ether, the stored guess.block becomes strictly greater than the current block number in the reference (it is set to block.number + 1), whereas the mutant sets it equal to the current block number and thus can be equal to block.number; this difference lets the mutant allow settling in the same block while the reference requires waiting one block.

After a successful lockInGuess by any actor sending 1 ether, the reference contract always stores a guess.block strictly greater than the current block (block.number + 1), whereas the mutant can store guess.block equal to the current block allowing settle() in the same block; the property asserts stored block > current block after lockInGuess for any fuzzed actor and hash.

After a successful lockInGuess call that sends exactly 1 ether, the reference C always records guesses(actor).block strictly greater than the block.number at the time of the call (block.number + 1), whereas the mutant sets it equal to block.number and thus can violate that strict inequality for some inputs.

After any successful lockInGuess call sending exactly 1 ether, the stored guesses(sender).block must be greater than the current block number at the time of the call; the mutant that stores block.number (not +1) can violate this by making stored block equal to the current block for some inputs.

For any caller and guess hash, after a successful lockInGuess call with exactly 1 ether the saved guesses(caller).block must be nonzero and strictly greater than the block.number at which settle would be called (i.e. settle cannot succeed in the same block); the mutant that stores block.number can make the stored block equal to the current block allowing settle to be callable in the same block, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with 1 ether when they previously had no guess, the stored block number for that caller is exactly current block.number + 1 (the reference always stores +1); the mutant that stores +2 breaks this rule for some inputs (block numbers) because it stores a different value.

After a successful lockInGuess call by any address sending exactly 1 ether when they had no prior guess, the stored mapping entry's block number equals the chain's current block number plus 1 (reference), whereas the mutant that sets +2 will violate this for callers at some block numbers.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess sending exactly 1 ether when they had no prior guess, the contract stores guesses[caller].block == block.number + 1; the mutant that sets +2 will cause this stored block to differ for some fuzzed caller and block states.

For any caller who had no prior guess and calls lockInGuess sending exactly 1 ether, the reference stores guesses[caller].block == block.number + 1 (the mutant stores +2 and will thus make the stored value != block.number + 1 for some inputs).

For any caller who had no prior guess and successfully calls lockInGuess sending exactly 1 ether, the reference contract records guesses[caller].block equal to the block at which they will be able to settle (i.e. block.number + 1), whereas the mutant that sets block.number + 2 stores a different future block and thus violates this equality for some inputs.

Reference requires settle() to only succeed in a block strictly after the locked block (so settling within the same block is impossible); the mutant allowing >= lets a caller settle in the same block they locked the guess and can thereby clear their guess and potentially receive funds earlier, violating that rule.

For any caller who successfully lockInGuess in block B, calling settle in the same block B must be disallowed (settle must revert or be unexecutable), ensuring guesses remain set; the mutant allowing settle in the same block breaks this by permitting a settle-call in block B that clears the guess (and may pay out).

For any caller who lockInGuess in block B, immediately after that call the guess remains set and calling settle in the same block must NOT clear the stored guess (i.e., settle invoked in the same block as the locked block either reverts or leaves guesses[msg.sender].block nonzero); the mutant allowing block.number >= storedBlock permits clearing in the same block and thus violates this invariant for some inputs.

For any caller who successfully lockInGuess in block B, immediately after that transaction the caller cannot successfully settle in the same block (settle must revert); the mutant changing '>' to '>=' allows settle to succeed in the same block for some inputs, breaking this invariant.

For any caller who lockInGuess(hash) in block B, calling settle() in the same block B must NOT change the contract's balance (i.e., not pay out funds); the mutant allowing >= can enable a payout in the same block and thus can reduce address(c).balance for some inputs.

For any caller who locked in a nonzero guess and later calls settle after the locked block, the reference contract preserves the stored guess value until after comparing with the computed answer (so the stored guess is only cleared after potential payout), whereas the mutant clears the guess before comparison causing the stored guess to become zero after settle and preventing payouts when the guess equals the answer.

For any caller who locked a nonzero guess and then calls settle after the target block, the reference preserves the stored guess until after comparing with the computed answer (so either the guess matched and the caller was paid or the guess remained stored until cleared), whereas the mutant clears the stored guess before comparing, causing the stored guess to become zero after settle and preventing payouts when the correct guess equals the answer.

For any caller who locked in a nonzero guess and later calls settle after the lock block, the contract preserves the stored guess value until after it computes and compares the answer (so the stored guess is only cleared after potential payout); the mutant clears the stored guess before comparison, causing the stored guess to be zeroed after settle for some inputs.

For any caller that successfully locked a nonzero guess, after calling settle the reference contract guarantees that the stored guess is only cleared after comparison (so if the guess equals the computed answer the contract pays out and the stored guess becomes zero as a result of settlement), whereas the mutant clears the stored guess before comparison causing the stored guess to be zeroed earlier and preventing payouts for some inputs.

For any caller who locked a guess and later calls settle after the target block, the correct contract either pays out 2 ether when the stored guess equals the computed answer (so address(c).balance decreases by 2 ether) or leaves state consistent; the mutant can zero the stored guess before comparison preventing a payout — so the universal rule: if a caller locked a nonzero guess that equals the computed answer, then after settle the contract's balance will have decreased by 2 ether (the mutant breaks this for some inputs).

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess and then calls settle (after the target block), the reference contract always clears the caller's stored guess.block to 0 after settle, whereas the mutant leaves guess.block non-zero when the payout occurs (i.e., if transfer succeeds), breaking the invariant that settle always resets the stored guess state.

After any caller successfully calls lockInGuess and later calls settle (with block progressed), the reference contract always clears guesses[caller].block to 0 regardless of payout; the mutant leaves guesses[caller].block non-zero when the payout occurs, so the stored block is not always cleared.

For any caller that successfully locked a guess and later calls settle after the target block, the reference contract always resets guesses[caller].block to 0 after settle; the mutant fails to clear it when the guess matches and a payout occurs (leaving guesses[caller].block nonzero).

For any caller who locked in a guess and later calls settle after the target block, the reference contract always clears guesses[caller].block to 0 after settle; the mutant leaves guesses[caller].block non-zero when the guess matches and a payout occurs, so the stored block remains nonzero in that case.

For any caller who locked a guess and later calls settle after the target block, the reference contract always clears guesses[caller].block to 0 after settle; the mutant keeps guesses[caller].block nonzero when the guess matches and the transfer succeeds, violating that invariant.
